seo_title: Indrid Cold: the Smiling Man of West Virginia, explained
seo_desc: Who Indrid Cold is, what Woodrow Derenberger said happened on Interstate 77 in November 1966, how John Keel turned him into the Grinning Man, the Mothman link, and where he shows up today.
summary: The smiling man in a glossy coat who Woodrow Derenberger said stepped out of a UFO in West Virginia in 1966.
body: On the evening of November 2, 1966, a salesman named Woodrow Derenberger said a craft shaped like an old kerosene lamp globe blocked his truck on Interstate 77 near Parkersburg, West Virginia. A man got out, walked over smiling, and talked to him without moving his lips. He said his name was Cold and that they meant no harm.

Derenberger told the story on local TV the next day and it blew up. Writer John Keel later tied it to Mothman and to a "grinning man" seen in New Jersey, and that's how a friendly visitor turned into one of the creepier figures in UFO lore.

p: Derenberger was driving home along I-77 a little before 7:30 at night when, he said, something that looked like an old kerosene lamp globe (flat bottom, dome on top) came down and blocked the road so he had to stop. A man stepped out. Derenberger described him as about six feet tall with an olive complexion, dark brown hair and a glossy dark blue coat, and said he had a smile on his face and seemed very courteous and friendly.

The man spoke to him telepathically. He told Derenberger not to be frightened and said something like "We come from a country that is not nearly as powerful as yours. We mean you no harm." They talked for about ten minutes, the man said he'd be in touch again, and then he went back to the craft and it took off.

Derenberger went to the police when he got home, and the next afternoon WTAP-TV in Parkersburg aired a 30-minute interview with him. After that other people started calling in about a man who fit the same description, and the local papers ran stories on it for about three weeks. Honestly it sounds like the whole valley was on edge that month, and with good reason given what was coming.

Derenberger didn't stop at one meeting. By 1969 he was saying he was in regular contact with the visitors and had flown to their home planet, Lanulos, twice. He gave lectures on it, went on the radio, and in 1971 his story came out as a book, Visitors from Lanulos, written with Harold W. Hubbard. In his version Cold was a kind, peaceful space brother, a lot closer to the [Nordic aliens](/creatures/nordic-aliens/) of the 1950s than anything scary. Derenberger died in 1990.

sections.h: How he became the Grinning Man
p: Here's where it gets murky. John Keel wrote about the case in his 1970 book Strange Creatures from Time and Space, in a chapter on what he called "the Grinning Man". Keel also told the story of two boys in Elizabeth, New Jersey who said that on October 11, 1966 they saw a very tall man in shiny green coveralls standing behind a fence, looking at them and grinning. Keel suggested the New Jersey man and Derenberger's visitor were the same being, and he's the one who gave the full name as Indrid Cold.

Skeptic Brian Dunning points out that Derenberger never actually described any strange grin. He said the man had a pleasant smile. The big unnatural grin came later, through Keel and the writers who followed him. Folklorist David Clarke has said Keel's line between fact and fiction was a very fine one, and in 2002 journalist John C. Sherwood found differences between what Keel wrote in letters at the time and what ended up in his books. So I'd take the grinning-demon version with a big grain of salt.

Derenberger's encounter was on November 2, 1966. The first big [Mothman](/creatures/mothman/) sighting at the TNT area outside Point Pleasant was on November 15, thirteen days later and about 70 miles down the Ohio River. Keel pulled both stories, plus the [Men in Black](/creatures/men-in-black/) and a lot of strange phone calls, into his 1975 book The Mothman Prophecies, and since then Indrid Cold and Mothman have pretty much been a package deal. Whether they have anything to do with each other besides timing is a whole other question, and I don't think there's any real evidence they do.

Cold shows up all over the place now. Bill Laing played him in the 2002 movie The Mothman Prophecies. A modern contactee in the second season of the documentary series Hellier (2019) claimed to be in touch with him. He was added to Fallout 76 in a 2023 update as a random encounter, alongside the game's Mothman. And a lot of people know him first from The Adventure Zone: Amnesty, the McElroy brothers' podcast, where Indrid Cold is the human disguise of a Mothman who can see the future (which, I'll admit, is a pretty great take on it).
If you're in the area, the [Mothman Museum](/places/mothman-museum/) in Point Pleasant is all about that strange stretch of 1966 and 1967.

faq.a: Indrid Cold is the name of the smiling man that Woodrow Derenberger said stepped out of a landed craft on Interstate 77 near Parkersburg, West Virginia on November 2, 1966. He's also known as the Grinning Man or the Smiling Man.

There's no evidence beyond Derenberger's own story. He was sincere enough to keep telling it for years, but he also went on to claim trips to another planet, and the creepy grinning version comes mostly from John Keel's books, which aren't the most reliable.

Not in the original stories. Derenberger's visitor was a smiling man in a coat, not a winged creature, and the two were only linked later by John Keel because they happened in the same area two weeks apart. The idea that Indrid Cold is Mothman in disguise comes from fiction, mainly The Adventure Zone podcast.
Lanulos is the planet Derenberger said Cold came from and that he later claimed to have visited twice. There's no known planet by that name.

faq.q: Why is he called the Grinning Man?
faq.a: John Keel called him that in his 1970 book, linking him to a tall grinning man two boys said they saw in Elizabeth, New Jersey in October 1966. Derenberger himself only said the man had a friendly smile.

faq.q: When did the Indrid Cold encounter happen?
faq.a: On the evening of November 2, 1966, a little before 7:30 PM, on Interstate 77 near Parkersburg, West Virginia. That's thirteen days before the famous first Mothman sighting in Point Pleasant.
